Subject: Request: monthly remedy cap and maintenance carveouts

Hi Lauren,

Thanks again for the productive demo last week. As we evaluate Redwood for transaction validation and real-time fraud checks, a couple of contract-level items popped up from procurement that we need to see reflected in the SLA template before Legal will greenlight a pilot. High level:

- We run high-volume, latency-sensitive flows during business hours for payments. We need clarity that the production uptime baseline and the monthly remedy calculation align with our risk model.
- We ask for a carveout for pre-scheduled maintenance windows (we can tolerate short maintenance if scheduled) and a separate carveout for emergency mitigation where a hard fail-safe is required.
- Most important: procurement wants a cap on monthly service credits, but also an escrow-style protection for large incidents so critical remediation funds aren’t exhausted by minor transient events.

I attached a short questionnaire that highlights what they care about (StellarPay-SLA-Questions.pdf). Can you propose an amendment we could include in the template that:
  1) defines standard uptime and latency buckets,
  2) proposes a monthly remedy cap (we currently see 25–40% in market), and
  3) explains an escrow or prioritized-credit approach for severe incidents?

Would appreciate a draft by EOD Wed — we have an internal review on Thu.

Best,
Elliot Harris
Head of Infrastructure, StellarPay
elliot.harris@stellarpay.com

Hi Elliot — thanks for the clear note and the questionnaire. Attaching a concise amendment that addresses each of the items you flagged (RBW-proposed-remedy-amendment.docx). High level plan below so your team can review quickly:

1) Uptime & latency buckets
   - Default hosted baseline: 99.95% monthly uptime for public-hosted plans.
   - Dedicated/Enterprise tier option: 99.99% with an agreed maintenance window policy.
   - Latency SLO: P95 token latency bands called out per route; we can include per-route thresholds as an appendix.

2) Monthly remedy structure (proposed)
   - Progressive credits: credits scale by outage severity band (0.5% credit for minor degradation up to 15% for prolonged full-region unavailability).
   - Monthly cap: propose a default cap of 25% of the monthly invoice as a starting point. This protects both parties and is in line with market norms for high-throughput infra.

3) Escrow / prioritized-credit safeguard
   - Proposal: create a "remedy escrow" pool equal to 50% of the monthly cap (i.e., 12.5% of monthly bill) that is reserved for incidents meeting the "severe" criteria (major data plane outage or data loss).
   - Credits for minor incidents draw from the standard credit band and do not consume the escrow. Escrow consumption requires severity review and is replenished monthly.

4) Maintenance carveouts
   - Pre-scheduled maintenance: scheduled maintenance < 8 hours per month is exempt if announced 72 hours in advance and limited to a 4-hour per-region window.
   - Emergency maintenance: limited carveout if an active incident requires immediate work to prevent data loss; such events are tracked with post-incident reports.

Next step: marked-up amendment attached. Quick question for procurement: would a 25% monthly cap with a 50% escrow (12.5% effective reserved) pass as an acceptable compromise, or do you need a higher escrow on contract signature? Happy to hop on a 30-minute call to walk through.

Best,
Lauren Bishop
Senior Account Executive, Redwood Inference
lauren_bishop@redwood.ai
Attachment: RBW-proposed-remedy-amendment.docx

Lauren — good draft. A few pragmatic guardrails from finance/ops perspective: 

- Financial cap: I can support 25% monthly cap for a pilot but from a contract risk perspective we should never exceed 30% without executive sign-off. Put that upper limit into the internal approval matrix.

- Escrow mechanics: I like the escrow idea but suggest we define: (a) escrow trigger = incident severity level S3 (multi-region outage OR confirmed data-plane loss) and (b) escrow draw approvals require Ops lead + Sales director sign-off within a 72-hour review window.

- Replenishment: escrow pool should replenish monthly; if the pool is consumed two months in a row, automatic exec escalation to consider temporary throttling of burst traffic or capacity adjustments.

- Maintenance windows: 72-hour notice is fine. Reduce the per-region default window to 3 hours unless the customer purchases an extended-maintenance SLA add-on. That keeps planned maintenance smaller and predictable.

- Implementation ops note: we should include fallback routing language — if a region is degraded, requests can be routed to a compatible region/model variant; credits should be applied only for requests that were routed but degraded in latency beyond the latency SLO.

If you want, I can redline the doc with these bullets.

-marcus

Elliot — thanks for the quick review window. We iterated internally and updated the amendment to incorporate operational and financial guardrails. Summary of the revised proposal (attached and summarized inline):

- Uptime: Hosted baseline 99.95% monthly; Dedicated option 99.99% (per-route latency SLOs remain an appendix).
- Remedy bands: progressive credits by severity band (minor/partial/major).
- Monthly cap: default 25% of monthly invoice. We will not exceed 30% without exec approval; this is explicitly stated in the amendment.
- Remedy escrow: 50% of the monthly cap reserved as an escrow (12.5% of bill) for incidents meeting the defined severity threshold (multi-region outage or confirmed data-plane loss).
- Escrow governance: an Ops + Sales director Severity Review within 72 hours is required to authorize escrow draws; escrow replenishes monthly. If escrow is depleted two months consecutively, the contract includes an automatic escalation clause.
- Maintenance carveouts: scheduled maintenance exempt if announced >=72 hours in advance and limited to 3 hours per region by default; emergency maintenance carveouts permitted when necessary to prevent data loss and will be accompanied by post-incident reports.

We also added explicit fallback routing language so credits apply only to traffic that experienced degraded latency beyond the agreed SLOs after routing options were exhausted.
